brief: Lane mm: push Metal batched decode of the 35B further, starting with an expert-grouped MoE kernel (read each expert's weights once per step), bitwise equal to the solo step per row; then the next lever from a B = 8 / 16 per-kernel profile (16-row GEMV tile or single-stream command-buffer overhead).
hypothesis: The MoE is about 24% of the B = 8 step and reads expert weights once per row; grouping rows by expert removes the repeated reads.

verdict: Row-exact fp8 (_xd, q(x) once, 4-row tile), fat-threadgroup MoE (per pair, 2 rows per simdgroup) and a one-row grid for narrow nvfp4 matrices cut the Metal 35B B = 8 step 31.4 to 21.3 ms; served aggregate +23 / +28 / +32% at 4 / 8 / 16 streams (512 generated), single stream +0.8%. Bitwise to the solo step; batching off byte-identical to main.
summary: Metal 35B batched decode: B = 8 step -32% in process, served 189.3 to 243.2 tok/s at 8 streams, bitwise; expert grouping itself measured slower than per-pair fat threadgroups.
lessons: The per-kernel profile labelled only the first dispatch of a multi-dispatch launch; the MoE was 42% of the B = 8 step, not 24%.

Reading each expert once (grouping pairs by expert) did not pay on Apple Silicon at B <= 8: only 27% of pairs share an expert, the cache catches the re-reads, and grouping serializes pairs. Fatter threadgroups (2 weight rows per simdgroup) gave the MoE win.
The staged multi-row fp8 GEMV re-quantized all rows of x per threadgroup into 32 KB of threadgroup memory; preparing q(x) once and reading it from device memory is bitwise and 25-40% faster per call.
A negative control must be checked against the data: a split scale fma is a no-op when a lane holds one block, and an in-block reorder is a no-op when the e2m1 x bf16 sum is exact.
Per-kernel mode inflates absolute GPU times about 1.5x; use shares, decide on wall time.
